title: Type complexity budgets and team conventions
hook: Type complexity budgets and team conventions shows up in everyday TypeScript and in senior interviews — this page explains what it is, why it matters, and how it behaves in the compiler versus JavaScript or C#.

blocks.text: Type complexity budgets and team conventions is a core concept in TypeScript. At run time, types erase — the engine still executes JavaScript — but at compile time this concept shapes safe APIs and catches bugs before deploy. This page explains the idea in plain English first, then shows small, explained examples you can run in the browser console or Node.js.

blocks.text: Senior interviews and production code both probe whether you understand Type complexity budgets and team conventions beyond syntax memorization. Misunderstanding here leads to subtle bugs — wrong equality results, leaked memory, untyped JSON boundaries, or async ordering surprises. If you know JavaScript, the comparison sections below help you transfer mental models instead of starting from zero.

blocks.title: Interview trap
blocks.body: Interviewers often ask "Type complexity budgets and team conventions" as a follow-up to a coding exercise. They want mechanism and tradeoffs — not a one-line definition.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Treating Type complexity budgets and team conventions as pure syntax without run-time behavior. Skipping validation at JSON or API boundaries. Saying "it works on my machine" without noting browser versus Node differences.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: add logging or DevTools breakpoints around Type complexity budgets and team conventions, write a failing test that captures the edge case, and explain tradeoffs aloud in design review. Senior interviewers want mechanism — what the compiler does — plus when not to use the clever version.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Hand-waving "Type complexity budgets and team conventions just works" without mentioning run-time checks, error paths, or comparison to JavaScript and C#. Cannot trace a concrete bug to this concept.
